newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl reassures Italy on EMU membership.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl reassures Italy on EMU membership.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl reassured Italy on Friday he had no objections to it joining Europe's planned monetary union, dismissing reports of a secret scheme to keep Rome out of the starting line-up for a single currency.
Kohl said the decision on which countries would be founding members of the new currency would only be taken early next year and no country could pre-judge the decision-making process.
"There is no question of this or that country passing judgment on which country will take part or not," he said after meeting Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi.

Britain's Financial Times reported earlier this week that European Union officials and central bankers were discussing a plan which would defer Italian entry, partly to assuage German fears that the new euro currency would be too soft.
"This is absolutely unacceptable," Kohl told a news conference, commenting on the report. "The German government is not doing this. This is wrong."
Prodi has pinned his political survival on getting Italy into the first wave of economic and monetary union (EMU), which is due to begin in 1999.
He echoed Kohl's comments that only the timetable and the economic criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty would determine who joined EMU. "Time will be the judge," he said.
"It's not a case of one country judging the other and then that's it," he added.

Although several European leaders have denied the plan exists, EU officials have told Reuters the idea was being considered by several governments. Germany has said bureaucrats may be discussing it but no political talks have taken place.

"Maybe the bureaucrats are discussing it. I'm not," Prodi told Reuters Financial Television after the summit. "If we join, we shall join with right and correct behaviour. We should be a strength for the union, not a problem."
Asked about comments from some members of his centre-right coalition on Italy's suitability to join EMU at the start, Kohl said they were not expressing the government line.

"Interests are being represented but these are not German interests -- those are in the (Maastricht) treaty. They are the timetable and the criteria," he said, adding both Italy and Germany would have to "do their homework" to make the grade.
Kohl accused the media of whipping up the story of a German-led campaign to defer Italian entry into EMU. "It's boring to say we've signed a treaty (and) will stick to it," he said.

In German newspaper interviews on Friday, Prodi cited Germany's commercial banks, its central bank -- the Bundesbank -- and the British press as the main forces in a campaign against Italian membership of EMU.
Kohl said potential candidates for EMU should not spend their time assessing other countries' suitability.
"Everyone should take care of their own back yard," the veteran chancellor said. "We as Germans must do a great deal ...so we can say that we have fulfilled the criteria."

German bankers at last weekend's world economic forum in Davos, Switzerland, raised the prospect of chaos in the financial markets if Italy joined EMU from the beginning, casting doubt on its economic credentials.
But some industrialists, who fear losing out in one their most important export markets, have pleaded for Italy to be included in EMU sooner rather than later.

Prodi said the two leaders had talked not just about EMU but about a wide range of subjects, particularly joblessness. "Both our countries have rates of unemployment above 12 percent," he said. "This is the dominant problem in Europe at the moment."
Several of Prodi's senior ministers accompanied him at the bilateral summit in the Bonn chancellery to hold talks with their German counterparts.
